Nov 5, 2026

Automatic retries for Durable Object calls

Durable ObjectsWorkers

The runtime now retries fetch() and RPC calls to a Durable Object when they fail with a retryable error before reaching it. This applies whether the caller is a Worker or another Durable Object. Short disruptions, such as brief network interruptions, no longer need a retry loop in your code.

By default, the runtime retries a call up to four times, and starts no retry more than 10 seconds after the initial call starts. It does not retry errors thrown by your Durable Object code, or errors with .overloaded set to true.

If the connection drops and the runtime cannot tell whether the Durable Object received the call, it still retries, but the Durable Object rejects the retry if the first attempt arrived. A method never runs twice because of a retry, unless you mark it with retryable() from cloudflare:durable-objects:

To change the limits for one stub, pass a retry option to get() or getByName(). maxRetries accepts 0 to 10 retries, and timeoutMs accepts 500 to 60,000 milliseconds:

If you already retry Durable Object calls in your own code, each of your attempts now includes the runtime's retries. Lower your own attempt count, or set maxRetries: 0 on stubs where your code handles retries.

To use retryable() and the retry option, update to Wrangler 4.158.0 or later.

For more information, refer to Automatic retries.

Nov 5, 2026

Set expiration dates for Email security policies

Email security

Email security now lets you set an expiration date when creating an allow or block policy. This helps you apply temporary policy changes without removing them manually.

After the selected date passes, the policy expires and no longer applies.

This feature is available to all Email security customers, regardless of plan.

Workers AI

We originally stated these models would be deprecated on November 15, 2026, and have moved the deprecation date to November 20, 2026.

Nov 4, 2026

Route across a pool of models with model aliases

AI Gateway

AI Gateway now supports model aliases. A model alias is a pool of models that your application calls by one name, such as custom/support-fast. AI Gateway tries the models in the order you set and falls back to the next one if a request fails, or uses smart routing to choose a model for each request.

Because your application only references the alias, you can swap models or change the routing algorithm on your gateway without redeploying. Create and manage aliases on your gateway's Routing page, alongside dynamic routes.

To call an alias through the REST API, use its name as the model. For example, send this body to /accounts/{account_id}/ai/run:

Include the cf-aig-gateway-id header to select the gateway where you created the alias. Aliases are scoped to individual gateways.

For setup instructions and routing options, refer to Model aliases.

Nov 4, 2026

Granular access controls for the top Personal Agents

Bots

The Configure AI bot policies setting is now named AI Crawler and Agent access policies.

Personal agents act on a person's behalf, fetching information or browsing in response to a request. The updated policies let you set actions for the top Personal Agents individually. This gives you control over agent access while allowing visitors to use agents to find answers or compare products using your site's content.

Customize how Personal Agents access your site via Security > Settings > AI Crawler and Agent access policies.

For more information, check out our blog ↗︎ or refer to our documentation for AI Crawler and Agent access policies.

Nov 4, 2026

Block data entry with Browser Isolation without losing search, copy, and zoom (beta)

Browser IsolationCloudflare One

Isolation policies now support a third keyboard option in beta: Allow read-only actions. Previously, the keyboard setting was binary — allow all input or block everything. With Allow read-only actions, you can block data entry while preserving the built-in browser actions your users depend on.

In Allow read-only actions mode, users can still find in page, select all, copy, print, and zoom. All other keyboard input is blocked from reaching the isolated page. Copy and print remain subject to their own policy settings, so the controls compose instead of overriding each other. For example, setting the keyboard to Allow read-only actions and copy to Do not allow lets users search and zoom but prevents them from copying content.

To use this feature, set Keyboard to Allow read-only actions in your isolation policy settings. Via the API, set keyboard to enable_read_only_actions in the biso_admin_controls object with version set to v2.

For more information, refer to Keyboard.

Nov 4, 2026

New managed rule to help mitigate CVE-2026-98432.

Cloudflare Network Firewall

Cloudflare Network Firewall has a new managed rule to help mitigate the Linux IPv4 TCP use-after-free vulnerability (CVE-2026-98432 ↗︎):

  • Rule name: Block CVE-2026-98432 ↗︎ traffic
  • Rule ID: 6a4df2bf984946a88c74b07349557e83

The rule is disabled by default. To use it:

  1. Go to Networking > Firewall Policies > Managed Rulesets.
  2. Enable the rule with action Log first.
  3. Review traffic that matches the rule.
  4. If the matching traffic is not expected for your environment, change the action to Block.

For more information on enabling managed rulesets, refer to Enable managed rulesets.

For more details about the vulnerability, including an agent assessment prompt and evidence sources, refer to the Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire briefing ↗︎.

Nov 4, 2026

Steer Cloudflare One users and private networks to the same endpoint with session affinity and hash steering in private load balancers

Load BalancingCloudflare TunnelCloudflare Mesh

Private load balancers can now keep each user on the same endpoint. This helps with applications that keep session state on a single server.

Two options are available:

  • Hash endpoint steering. In the dashboard, set a pool's Endpoint steering to Hash. Each user is mapped to an endpoint within the pool.
  • Session affinity. With the API, set session_affinity to ip_cookie on the load balancer. Each user stays on the same endpoint while it remains healthy and your pools do not change. Refer to Session affinity.

For traffic from the Cloudflare One Client, Cloudflare identifies the user by their device, so a user stays on the same endpoint even if their IP address changes. For other traffic, such as from a Cloudflare WAN site, Cloudflare uses the source IP address.

This works for endpoints reached through Cloudflare Tunnel, Cloudflare Mesh, and Cloudflare WAN. Affinity pins the endpoint, not the cloudflared or Mesh replica that carries the traffic.

To learn how private load balancing fits with your connectors, refer to Load balance private network traffic.

Workers

Requests can require different amounts of work. A product lookup might be cheap, while a search runs an expensive database query. Use weighted requests to make expensive operations consume more of the same rate limit.

The Rate Limiting binding now accepts an optional delta in limit(). Pass delta to choose how many units a call consumes.

For example, assign one unit to a product lookup and 10 units to an expensive search. Both operations consume the same user's allowance. The following handler takes a verified user ID from your application's authentication flow:

The delta defaults to 1. To use delta in local development, use Wrangler 4.157.0 ↗︎ or later. For TypeScript support, use @cloudflare/workers-types version 5.20261106.1 or later.

For more details, refer to Weighted requests.

Nov 3, 2026

Agents SDK now supports Pi 1.5 with fewer storage writes and lower memory use

Agents

Agents SDK v0.33.0 upgrades PiHarness to Pi 1.5 ↗︎. The release reduces storage transactions while streaming, improves throughput across many sessions, and reduces memory use when streaming large tool calls.

Performance improvements

  • Far fewer storage writes while streaming. Pi stores streamed answers and tool output in batches, within a second of each update, instead of on every update. Over SQLite, this cuts storage transactions by about 27x for long answers and 5.7x for turns with parallel tools, and CPU by about a quarter.
  • Higher throughput across many sessions. Pi's scheduler no longer rechecks every conversation on each commit. In a SQLite benchmark with 2,048 sessions, one Pi harness went from 88 to 459 agent runs per second.
  • Less memory on large answers. Streaming a 500 KB tool call used to take about 20 seconds of CPU and a 100 MB heap. Pi now appends new text instead of copying it on every update.

Streaming updates remain visible immediately, but are persisted in batches. With the default settings, a crash can lose up to about one second of streamed progress. Refer to Recovery to configure this interval.

Session and tool updates

  • A view of each session. session.watch() replaces session.events(). It returns the newest transcript entries and the session's live state, such as the answer being streamed, running tools, and why the last run ended without an answer.
  • Continue without adding a message. The new session.continue() API starts a new run using the existing transcript, for example after a model error or when a run reaches its turn limit.
  • Turn limit. defaults.maxTurns caps the tool rounds a run can take in new sessions.
  • Tasks that keep crashing end. Pi now ends a task cut off by its restart limit instead of parking it. retry() and the parked status are removed.
  • Browser in Pi's code mode. Scripts in Pi's code mode can call browserTool and pass its screenshots to image(). browserTool also stops when the harness aborts its call.

Continue an unanswered conversation

For an existing session and submission operationId, check the result before offering a continuation. For example, after resolving a model error:

This starts a new run without appending a user message. The session must be idle. If the transcript already ends in an answer, the operation returns unanswered with reason nothing_to_answer. Refer to Work with sessions.

Upgrade

Once a conversation runs on Pi 1.5, Pi 1.4 cannot read it. After upgrading, roll forward to fix deployment issues rather than rolling back to Pi 1.4.

Update callers of session.events() to use session.watch(), and remove uses of retry() and the parked status. Refer to the Pi Durable 1.5.0 changelog ↗︎ for the full list of breaking changes.

The Agents SDK v0.33.0 changelog ↗︎ has step-by-step upgrade instructions. Point your coding agent at them and upgrade today:

Nov 3, 2026

New AI Gateways require authentication

AI Gateway

New AI Gateways now require authentication to prevent unauthorized requests. Once authentication is on, you cannot turn it off through the dashboard or API.

When you create a new AI Gateway through the API, authentication is on by default. You can leave out the authentication field or set it to true. If you set it to false, the API returns HTTP 400.

When you update an existing gateway, leaving out authentication keeps its current setting. If you try to turn off authentication after it is on, the API returns HTTP 400.

Existing gateways with authentication turned off can continue without it. You can turn it on in your gateway settings or include authentication: true in a gateway update request:

Before turning authentication on, configure HTTP clients to send a valid Cloudflare API token. Requests through Workers bindings remain pre-authenticated.

For setup instructions and supported authorization headers, refer to AI Gateway authentication.

Nov 3, 2026

See which AI assistants act for your users in Account Abuse Protection

Bots

Account Abuse Protection now shows when a recognized AI assistant makes a login or sign up request, and which account it was acting for.

  • Population overview: See which AI assistants are active across your users and how many accounts use them.
  • Account activity: Every login and sign up event shows whether an AI assistant made the request, and which one.
  • AI assistant filters: filter accounts by number of AI assistant events or number of AI assistants.

Use this to investigate and mitigate a single account without blocking an assistant for everyone else who relies on it, and to tune your agent settings in AI Crawler and Agent access policies.

AI assistant visibility covers login and sign up events only. Requests from assistants that Cloudflare does not recognize appear as ordinary traffic.

For more information, refer to AI assistants.

Nov 3, 2026

Crawl results include URL outcomes and robots.txt diagnostics

Browser Run

Browser Run /crawl results now include more detailed diagnostics. Each URL record can include an outcome that identifies the specific processing result, such as success, robots_disallowed, timeout, or page_error.

The job-level robots array reports the robots.txt state for up to 50 origins encountered by the crawl. Each entry includes the origin, whether usable rules were available, and the HTTP status when the crawler received a response.

For field definitions and all possible outcome values, refer to URL outcomes and robots.txt diagnostics.

Nov 3, 2026

Zero Wire, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities

Radar

Cloudflare Radar now includes Zero Wire ↗︎, a hub for investigating critical Internet vulnerabilities and threats. Each briefing separates confirmed facts from open questions, lists remediation steps, and shows what Cloudflare observes about the threat.

Briefings

Briefings are grouped by urgency. Needs attention covers active incidents, new guidance, or unresolved scope that security teams should review now. Reference keeps stable briefings available, even if not every affected system has been patched. Each card shows the recommended action and summarizes what happened, why it matters, and what to do.

Each briefing page expands on the card with an update chronology and an overview, followed by:

  • What to do now: remediation steps, plus a prompt to copy into an AI agent with access to your infrastructure, asking for an evidence-based assessment of affected systems and exposure.
  • Cloudflare coverage: the Cloudflare products that protect against the threat, and any impact on Cloudflare's own services.
  • Evidence and sources: vendor advisories, CVE records, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, and Radar charts, such as requests matching the related Cloudflare WAF rules.

Follow updates

Search briefings by CVE, name, or tag, or browse every briefing with a given tag. To follow new briefings and updates, subscribe to the Zero Wire RSS feed ↗︎ or to the feed of a single tag. New briefings also appear in the Caught on Radar ↗︎ section of the Radar homepage.

Send questions or feedback from any briefing page, or at radar@cloudflare.com.

For more details, read the blog post ↗︎ or visit Zero Wire ↗︎.

Nov 2, 2026

AI Search billing postponed to December 1, 2026, and default sync interval is now 24 hours

AI Search

Billing postponed to December 1, 2026

AI Search billing has been postponed by one month and now begins on December 1, 2026, instead of November 1, 2026. You will not be charged for AI Search usage before December 1, 2026. Pricing and included usage are unchanged.

For rates and included usage, refer to Limits & pricing.

Default sync interval is now 24 hours

The default sync interval for AI Search instances is changing from 6 hours to 24 hours. You can still choose any supported interval, from 15 minutes to 24 hours, with the Sync interval setting in your instance settings or the sync_interval field in the API.

For details, refer to Sync interval.

Nov 2, 2026

New Account Abuse Protection Dashboard

Bots

Account Abuse Protection customers in Early Access can now investigate login and sign up activity in a dedicated dashboard under Security > Account Abuse Protection.

  • Population overview: See total login and sign up events, unique accounts, IPs and devices, top countries and ASNs, and leaked credential check results. Filter accounts by signals such as leaked credential events and unique IPs to find the accounts that need review.
  • Individual Account overview: Review a single Hashed User ID's activity, including its top networks, locations and devices, and an event log with the Ray ID for each event. Mitigate the account with a Security Rule on its Hashed User ID.
  • New roles: The Account Abuse Protection role grants access to the dashboard. Account Abuse Protection PII role grants access to the dashboard as well as account-level PII, such as email address, and is required to create or edit Logpush jobs that include PII. The dashboard includes all login and sign up events from the date the feature was enabled.

For more information, refer to Account Abuse Protection.

Nov 2, 2026

Organize and authorize Access service tokens with tags

Cloudflare OneAccess

You can now assign key-value tags to Access service tokens and use those tags to organize credentials or control application access. Each token supports up to five tags, such as environment: production or team: payments.

Add or edit tags when you create or update a token in the dashboard or service token API. You can search and filter by tag on the Service Tokens page. Tags also appear in Resource Tagging, where you can query them alongside other tagged resources.

The Service Token Tag policy selector matches valid tokens with an exact key-value pair. Use it in a Service Auth policy to authorize tokens by environment or team without listing each token individually. For example, this API policy configuration accepts valid tokens tagged environment: production:

For setup instructions, refer to Tag service tokens and Authorize service tokens by tag.

Nov 2, 2026

Evaluate Flagship flags locally

Flagship

Flagship bindings now evaluate flags against a local flag store during local development, instead of calling your remote app. You can develop offline and test flag changes without affecting production. This applies to wrangler dev, the Cloudflare Vite plugin, the Vitest integration, and cf dev.

The local store starts empty, so evaluations return the default value you pass in code. Add and manage local flags in any of these ways:

  • Wrangler — Add --local to wrangler flagship flags commands, such as create, update, and evaluate. To copy all flags from your remote app, run npx wrangler flagship flags pull <APP_ID>.
  • Local Explorer — Create, edit, toggle, and evaluate flags in Local Explorer while your dev server runs.
  • cf CLI — Add --local to cf flagship commands.

To keep evaluating against your remote app instead, set remote: true on the binding.

The local flag store requires Wrangler v4.135.0 or @cloudflare/vite-plugin v1.56.0 or later. Flagship in Local Explorer requires Wrangler v4.148.0 or @cloudflare/vite-plugin v1.63.0 or later.

Refer to Flagship local development for details.

Nov 2, 2026

Workers will use the new module registry by default on November 17

Workers

Starting November 17, 2026, JavaScript Workers with a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later will use the new module registry by default. You will no longer need the new_module_registry flag for these dates. Python Workers keep using the legacy registry.

The module registry finds and loads JavaScript modules in your Worker. We announced the new registry in September 2026 ↗︎. It improves compatibility with JavaScript standards and Node.js. In Workers using Node.js compatibility, you can use require() to load ES modules. The module and its dependencies must not use top-level await.

You can also use import.meta to get information about the current module and find the URL of another module without loading it:

When deployed with src/index.ts as the unbundled entrypoint, isEntrypoint is true. helperUrl is a URL within your Worker bundle. Resolving the URL does not check whether the module exists or load it over the network. Build tools may transform import.meta. To try this example directly, refer to unbundled deployments.

Existing Workers keep their current behavior until you change their compatibility date or flags. To try the new registry before November 17, keep your current date and add new_module_registry to your compatibility flags.

Before updating, check your dependencies for invalid import attributes and changes to require() behavior. The new registry rejects invalid import attributes. Calls to require() also fail if the module or any of its dependencies use top-level await. To keep the legacy registry with a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later, add legacy_module_registry.

For migration details, refer to the new module registry compatibility flag, bundling documentation, and Node.js compatibility documentation.

Nov 2, 2026

Request.signal will be enabled by default in Workers on November 17

Workers

Starting November 17, 2026, Workers with a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later will receive client disconnection events through request.signal by default. Use these events to stop unnecessary work when a client leaves. You will no longer need the enable_request_signal compatibility flag for these dates.

We introduced this feature in May 2025. You can log cancellations, clean up resources, or cancel operations that accept an AbortSignal.

For example, this Worker logs a client disconnection and cancels an outgoing request:

Existing Workers keep their current behavior until you change their compatibility date or flags. To try this feature before November 17, keep your current date and add enable_request_signal to your compatibility flags.

With a compatibility date of 2026-11-17 or later, add disable_request_signal to opt out. This change does not enable request_signal_passthrough. Pass the signal explicitly, as the example does.

For more information, refer to the Request API and the Request.signal compatibility flag.

Oct 30, 2026

Inspect provisioned users and groups with the SCIM population viewer

Cloudflare OneAccess

The SCIM population viewer lets you inspect the users and groups provisioned to Cloudflare One by each identity provider. You can check which resources Cloudflare has received without making API requests or opening a support ticket.

In Zero Trust > Integrations > Identity providers, select a user or group count in SCIM resources to open the viewer. You can:

  • Search users by username, email, name, or resource ID, and groups by name or resource ID.
  • Inspect resource attributes in formatted or JSON views.
  • View group members and compare Cloudflare and IdP resource IDs with provisioning logs.
  • Delete individual resources from the Cloudflare SCIM population when you have edit permission.

The viewer shows provisioned resources rather than provisioning event history. Use SCIM provisioning logs to investigate failed requests. Existing SCIM deprovisioning and policy behavior remain unchanged.

For dashboard instructions and API examples, refer to View SCIM users and groups.
